newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: East Asia jet fuel export to US dries up supplies.
newsitem.headline: East Asia jet fuel export to US dries up supplies.

text.p: Rare jet fuel winter cargo movements from South Korea and Japan to the U.S. West Coast have helped to exhaust supplies in Asia and boosted prices, oil industry sources said on Friday.

They said tight prompt supplies of jet fuel in the U.S. West Coast have resulted in higher prices there compared with East Asia over the past one to two weeks, encouraging South Korean and Japanese sellers to ship cargoes westward.
One Korean refiner has been particularly active in exporting cargoes westwards, traders said.
East Asian barrels were also in demand in Hawaii, they said.
Jet fuel cargoes were sold to the West Coast at around $1.00 per barrel above Singapore spot quotes free-on-board (fob) basis from South Korea and Japan, traders said.
Prices in Japan and Korea on an fob basis is currently around $1.20 per barrel premium to Singapote spot quotes.

"A number of players in the Far East are also short into the U.S. West Coast, but there are no cargoes," one Korean trader said. "There are also those who are short into Japan who can't find cargoes."
A refiner in Singapore said: "Ironically we have been cutting refinery runs and the availabilities of jet have been limited...despite refiners maximising jet production over gas oil."
But they noted that the rally in jet fuel price in Asia this week has made it uneconomical to continue to move the limited number of cargoes to the U.S.
Traders said fob Singapore price currently averages $30.60 a barrel while waterborne U.S. West Coast price averages $34.44 a barrel.
Traders said Asian jet fuel became attractive for U.S. buyers when prices started to slip along with gas oil, from $33.25 a barrel on January 8 to below $28.00 on January 22.
This coincided with a fire at Tosco Corp's 156,000-barrel-per-day (bpd) refinery in Martinez California on January 21, which resulted in a severe tightness for prompt barrels, traders said.
Jet fuel prices in Asia also soared over the past week because of active purchases by Indonesia for February delivery cargoes.
Indonesia has bought about 1.5 million barrels so far and traders said they might take another one or two cargoes.
Traders said the market has also been pushed too high by a Singapore trader whom they said is pricing their cargo sales into Indonesia.
The trader this week bought two cargoes totalling 250,000 barrels for mid-to-second half February lifting at $30.40 and $30.75 per barrel, fob Singapore.
But traders said fob jet fuel price is not expected to breach the $31.00 mark even though demand is expected to remain healthy into the first half of March.
